ety.text: Proto-Germanic *bō-redup. Proto-Germanic *babô Proto-West Germanic *babō Old English *baba Middle English babe Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y Middle English baby English baby From Middle English baby, babie (“baby”), a diminutive form of babe (“babe, baby”), equivalent to babe + -y/-ie (“endearing and diminutive suffix”). Perhaps ultimately imitative of baby talk (compare babble).

senses.d: A very young human, particularly from birth to a couple of years old or until walking is fully mastered.
ex: In that film, I often hid my head in my hands, unable to watch scenes about dead babies and diving into gruesome lavatories.

senses.d: A very young human, even if not yet born.
ex: When is your baby due?
Her baby had always been active, even before he was born, when he would kick her bladder.

senses.d: Any very young animal, especially a vertebrate; many species have specific names for their babies, such as kittens for the babies of cats, puppies for the babies of dogs, and chicks for the babies of birds. See :Category:Baby animals for more.
A person who is immature, infantile, or feeble.
ex: Stand up for yourself – don't be such a baby!

senses.d: A person who is new to or inexperienced in something.
ex: I only qualified as an architect this summer, so I'm still a baby.

senses.d: The lastborn of a family; the youngest sibling, irrespective of age.
ex: Adam is the baby of the family.
"He's a year older than me." "You're the baby, eh?"

senses.d: A person's romantic partner; a term of endearment used to refer to or address e.g. one's girlfriend, boyfriend, or spouse.
ex: Too busy thinking about my baby, and I ain't got time for nothing else.
Baby, don't cry.

senses.d: A form of address to a person considered to be attractive.
ex: Hey baby, what are you doing later?

senses.d: A thing that is comparatively small of its kind.
A concept or creation endeared by its creator.
ex: This test program I've designed is my new baby.

senses.d: Picked when small and immature (as in baby corn, baby potatoes).
Newest (overall, or in some group or state); most inexperienced.
Like or pertaining to a baby, in size or youth; small, young.
ex: Spider. Here let us begin at the beginning, at the babyest of books for Edith's nursery.
A doll show held the attention of children at Allen as a special feature during the week. Winners were:[…]baby-est doll, Betty McQueary.

senses.d: To coddle; to pamper somebody like an infant.
ex: […] though he tried to be gruff and mature, he yielded to her and was glad to be babied.

senses.d: To tend (something) with care; to be overly attentive to (something), fuss over.

grp.label: very young human being — see also child
term of endearment — see also darling
form of address to a man or a woman considered to be attractive

ety.text: Inherited from Old French petit, from Vulgar Latin pittitus (775; compare Latin pitinnus, pitulus). Compare Spanish pequeño.

Nickname given to Nicolas Ferry, renowned throughout Europe as the court dwarf of the Polish King Stanisław Leszczyński. Possibly derived from bab- (babiller, babine) rather than adapted from English baby, although this may have contributed to the diffusion of the word.

Uncertain. Possibly from: * An onomatopoeic root or children's/nursery word *pikk-, *picc-. * From Vulgar Latin *pikk (“little”), related to *piccāre (“to pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”). * From picca (“point”).
Probably from Vulgar Latin *cattulus (“whelp, puppy”), from Latin catŭlus (“puppy”). Compare with Portuguese cachorro.
From filho (“son”) + -ote.

fr:nourrisson.gl: infant; baby; nursling (a child who breastfeeds)

ety.text: Inherited from Late Latin *nūtrītiōnem (distinct from the abstract noun nūtrītiō), from nūtrītus, past participle of nūtriō.

it:bambino.gl: child, baby, toddler, tot (male or of unspecified gender)

ety.text: Onomatopoeic bambo for the first stammerings of children, plus -ino (diminutive suffix).
Variant of bambino (“child”).
Borrowed from French bébé.
Onomatopoeic; compare niño (“boy”).
See bebé.
Borrowed from French bébé.
Unknown, though probably related to Vulgar Latin *ninnus.
From the biblical character Benjamin.
From the biblical Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob.
The second sense is probably from Benjamin Electric Manufacturing Company, an American company that made early electrical accessories like adaptors.
Inherited from Old French chous, from Latin caulis, itself akin to or derived from Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós).
Substantivization of the singular feminine form of bello (“beautiful”).
Inherited from Latin bellus.

es:nena.gl: babe, dear (term of endearment to a woman or girl)

ety.text: Feminine form of nene (“kid, baby”).
From doce + -inho.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bel, from Latin bellus, from Proto-Indo-European *dw-ene-, adverbial form of *deu- (“to do, perform, revere, show favor”).

As one of the first utterances many babies are able to say, baba (like mama, papa, and dada) has come to be used in many languages as a term for various family members: * father: Albanian, Arabic, Western Armenian, Chinese, Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi, Bengali, Greek, Marathi, Marshallese, Mingrelian, Nepali, Persian, Swahili, Turkish, Yoruba, Shona, Zulu * grandmother: many Slavic languages (such as Bulgarian, Czech, Russian, Serbo-Croatian and Polish; a doublet of bubbe), Romanian, Yiddish, Japanese * grandfather: Azerbaijani, Zulu (father, grandfather) * baby: Afrikaans, Sinhala, Hungarian These t…

senses.d: A kind of sponge cake soaked in rum-flavoured syrup.
A grandmother.
ex: My baba, Ksenia Dubinsky, tells me that my education makes her proud.

senses.d: An old woman, especially a traditional old woman from an Eastern European culture.
ex: Only two women, typical "babas" (peasant women) in the house from which I got my quilt and bedcloth, could be coaxed to pose;

senses.d: A father.
ex: "The greatest gift and honor is having you for a daughter. I've missed you so." "I've missed you too, baba."
Okay. Okay. Fine, baba. Let's just do it before something else goes wrong.

senses.d: A holy man, a spiritual leader.
ex: While I was in Port Alberni, three babas came to Canada to raise money ...
Most babas had little contact with written culture and are not therefore named in books and treatises.

senses.d: A baby, child.
ex: For my child is dead—my baba is dead!

senses.d: In baby talk, often used for a variety of words beginning with b, such as bottle or blanket.
ex: Oh, it's storytime! Let me get my baba.

ety.text: Proto-Germanic *bō-redup. Proto-Germanic *babô Proto-West Germanic *babō Old English *baba Middle English babe English babe From Middle English babe, a variant of earlier baban, perhaps from Old English *baba (“boy, child”), from Proto-West Germanic *babō, from Proto-Germanic *babô, reduplicated variant of *ba-, *bō- (“father, brother, close male relation”). cognates and related terms Related to Old Frisian bobba (“child”) (whence North Frisian babbe, babb, babe (“child”)), Old High German Babo (a male forename), see boy. Otherwise, origin obscure. Compare mama, dada, papa.

senses.d: A baby or infant; a very young human or animal.
ex: These events came to pass when he was but a babe.

Though he possess sweet babes and loving wife,
A home of peace by loyal friendships cheered,
And love them more than death or happy life,

senses.d: An attractive person, especially a young woman.
ex: She's a real babe!

senses.d: A darling (a term of endearment).
ex: Hey, babe, how's about you and me getting together?
But, Babe, you don't have to meet 'em if you don't want to.

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese gata, from Late Latin catta.
